title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator Suite for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). Outcomes were binary per task (validator pass/fail). Results: baseline (single‑pass) 299/300 passes, guarded (GVR) 300/300 passes; paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Provider_call_audit records stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and total model_calls_used = 301, i.e., the registered repair stage executed only once under the preregistered repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially increases pass rate (target effect 0.10 with planned ≈80% power at N=300) was not supported. We interpret this as a ceiling effect combined with minimal GVR engagement, explicitly document model and orchestration settings, summarize the shared‑initial paired design and repair trigger logic, and point readers to the sealed preregistration and archived execution artifacts for full per‑task diagnostics and provider traces.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for automating NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and change planning. Prior work shows LLM outputs can contain syntax, topology, or semantic errors and that combining generation with deterministic verifiers and iterative repair can reduce such errors. However, the community lacks a standardized, machine‑checkable benchmark that (i) couples synthetic but operationally structured intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and (ii) supports sealed confirmatory comparisons of defended pipelines (GVR) versus single‑pass generation. To address this gap we preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to test whether a guarded GVR pipeline produces a materially higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass LLM under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget. Our contributions: (1) a sealed preregistered benchmark design and deterministic validator specification; (2) an autonomous execution of a paired N=300 confirmatory comparison (ac-2026-003-prereg-v1) using declared model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0); (3) a complete archival bundle (preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts) supporting community reuse and extension. The final research question: Can a standardized synthetic task set and deterministic validator reveal a material per‑task correctness advantage for an automated GVR pipeline over a frozen single‑pass LLM under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget?
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and technical studies document active interest in LLMs for NetOps and repeatedly highlight evaluation, realism, and safety gaps [Long et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024]. Empirical work shows LLMs can synthesize router configurations but often require verifier assistance to avoid misconfigurations [Mondal et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024]; generate–validate–repair architectures and context‑aware iterative prompting have been proposed to increase correction rates [Jiang et al., 2024]. Security analyses highlight prompt injection, jailbreaks, and hallucination risks that are relevant to operational workflows [Shen et al., 2024; Greshake et al., 2023]. These studies motivate a sealed, artifact‑grounded confirmatory comparison using machine‑checkable correctness semantics rather than only language‑level metrics.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and hypothesis. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass LLM on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). Design. We used a paired binary design in which a single shared initial generation candidate was produced per task and used as the baseline single‑pass candidate. The guarded condition reuses the same initial candidate, runs the deterministic validator, and—only if the validator reports failure—may perform up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This shared‑initial design isolates repair effectiveness by controlling generation variance: baseline and guarded initially see the identical candidate, so differences can only arise from the guarded repair stage. Task bank and validator. A deterministic task generator produced 300 intent→configuration tasks evenly distributed across four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, and workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints). The validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0) implements the scoring rule “full_intent_constraint_validation”, emits structured diagnostics, and returns score=1 with score_reason_code=VALID_CONFIGURATION only when all declared constraints are satisfied. Model and generation settings. Declared and used model (execution/model_configuration.json): declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"; provider = "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. The null temperature indicates the execution adapter relied on the hosted model's deterministic sampling mode under the recorded provider settings; seeding and single shared call semantics ensured identical shared initial outputs between baseline and guarded (see execution/provider_call_audit recorded in the archived execution manifest). Preregistered analysis. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on N=300 paired binary outcomes. The pre‑specified test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test with a paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) to produce a percentile 95% CI. Exclusion rules removed ambiguous specifications or contamination; none occurred. All seeds, provider traces, and per‑task validator outputs are archived and cited below.
sections.results: Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600 (300 shared initial generation calls + up to 300 repair attempts), model_calls_used = 301, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 300. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation) records stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}; therefore the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks under the preregistered repair budget. Primary aggregated results (analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0); contingency n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. Interpretation. The observed pattern—very high baseline pass rate with a single discordant guarded‑only success—yields no evidence that the guarded pipeline produced a materially higher pass rate under the preregistered target effect (0.10). The small and imbalanced discordant counts produce an exact McNemar p that does not reject symmetry; the bootstrap CI includes 0, consistent with a negligible observed paired difference.
sections.discussion: Why GVR showed no confirmatory advantage here. Two interlocking factors explain the null confirmatory outcome on this benchmark: (1) ceiling effect—single‑pass baseline already satisfied validator constraints on 299/300 tasks, leaving little room for measurable improvement relative to the preregistered 0.10 target effect; (2) minimal GVR engagement—because the validator passed nearly all shared initial candidates, the guarded repair stage was invoked only once (repair stage_counts = 1). Together these factors mean the paired comparison largely contrasted identical initial candidates rather than actively repaired outputs. Implications for benchmark design. This negative/ceiling outcome demonstrates the importance of aligning task difficulty, validator strictness, and repair budget with the planned sensitivity of confirmatory tests. To better reveal repair benefits one can (a) increase task difficulty or the prevalence of validator‑failing initial candidates, (b) allow larger repair budgets or iterative repairs, (c) adopt stateful temporal validators or emulation that model in‑flight dynamics, or (d) evaluate multiple model generations per task to widen generation variance. Repair trigger and repair trace locus. Repair trigger policy (preregistered): guarded invokes a repair call iff the deterministic validator returns a failing score for the shared initial candidate and the per‑task repair budget allows a repair (here, ≤1). The execution manifest and provider_call_audit record that only one repair invocation occurred; the full repair provider trace (provider request, provider response, and recorded timestamps) and its artifact hash are archived in the execution bundle under execution/provider_calls/ and are indexed by the execution/execution_manifest.json and the full artifact hash manifest. For readers who wish to inspect the single repair episode in full, the archived execution manifest and provider_calls directory contain the immutable provider trace and SHA‑256 hash (see archival pointers in the Disclosure Statement below). Representative failure diagnostics and task difficulty. The per‑task validator traces (execution/scoring/*.json) include the validator diagnostics (violation_codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration) for every task. Detailed counts of task difficulty levels and the full identifier and validator diagnostic for the sole baseline failure are recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/scoring/*.json and are made available in the archived bundle; these artifacts are the authoritative source for the requested per‑task diagnostic values. In the submission bundle we also include a small set of representative tasks with explicit difficulty labels to illustrate the task encoding format (examples shown in the paper's artifact_examples). Threats to validity and limitations are discussed below.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed, reproducible synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported on this task set. Critically, the guarded repair stage executed only once (repair stage_counts = 1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable community extensions (harder tasks, stateful validators, larger repair budgets, multi‑model comparisons) that can better evaluate where GVR pipelines yield measurable operational value.

disclosure_statement: This study followed the sealed preregistration ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765) and used archived execution and analysis artifacts. Declared model and generation settings (from execution/model_configuration.json): declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"; provider = "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null (hosted adapter deterministic sampling mode was used); these settings governed both baseline and guarded shared initial generation. Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 implemented the shared initial generation (single shared call per task) and the guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implementing the scoring rule labeled "full_intent_constraint_validation"; per‑task scorer outputs are archived under execution/scoring/*.json. Initial master prompt: archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy: a human Research Director selected the topic family and provided pre‑lock constraints; after the autonomy lock the autonomous pipeline performed literature synthesis, study selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revision. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Execution accounting (authoritative): planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, completed_pair_count = 300, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call). Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}; thus the guarded repair stage executed only once under the preregistered repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The single repair provider trace (provider request/response and timestamps) and its SHA‑256 are archived in the execution bundle under the provider_calls directory and are indexed by execution/execution_manifest.json and the full artifact hash manifest contained in the bundle. All artifacts cited in this paper (notably: execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/scoring/*.json, execution/responses/*.txt, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv) are included in the archived submission bundle and are the authoritative provenance for the empirical claims above.
limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot, task‑declared workflow_policies and required sequences but does not model temporal in‑flight dynamics, vendor execution idiosyncrasies, or runtime side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture full production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) limit sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain the confirmatory inference regarding practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further multi‑model experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving planned exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider conditions recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the execution manifest.

Requested per‑task summary values: exact counts by difficulty level across the full N=300 and the exact identifier and validator diagnostic for the single baseline failure are present in the archived execution artifacts (execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/scoring/*.json). Those artifact files are authoritative. Because this revision incorporated all artifact‑backed, non‑sensitive details that were present in the provided manuscript evidence bundle (notably model configuration, stage_counts, and the per‑condition aggregated counts), and because the full per‑task provider trace SHA‑256 for the single repair invocation is recorded in the archived execution manifest/provider_calls index, readers should consult the archived execution bundle for the immutable per‑task identifiers and trace hashes (the submission bundle contains execution/execution_manifest.json and the full artifact hash manifest). If journal/panel reviewers require we will include an explicit short table of per‑difficulty counts and the single failed task’s identifier/validator diagnostic verbatim, we will do so only if the corresponding fields are extracted directly from the archived execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/scoring/*.json artifacts and referenced by their artifact hashes.
